**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** [Current date]

Over the past few weeks we've been debating a question that keeps resurfacing whenever someone waits more than a few minutes for a fine-tuning job: do we buy more local AI hardware, or do we get more out of the machines we already own? I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because I don't believe the answer is obvious, and I want us to decide it deliberately rather than by default.

The case for buying more hardware is the easiest to make emotionally. Our queue times spike at exactly the moments we can least afford them — the days before a demo, the week a model needs retraining after a data incident. Every one of those delays has a real cost, not just in engineer hours but in the experiments we quietly decide not to run because "the cluster is busy." That last category is the one that worries me most, because it's invisible. We never see the model improvement we didn't attempt. Opportunity cost of this kind doesn't show up in any dashboard, and it compounds: a team that learns to route around its own infrastructure slowly stops asking ambitious questions of it.

But before we reach for a purchase order, we should be honest about what our current hardware is actually doing. The utilisation data we pulled last month tells a less dramatic story than our queue-time complaints do. Average utilisation sits in the mid-thirties, with long idle stretches overnight and on weekends, punctuated by bursts where we're genuinely saturated. That pattern is typical of small teams, and it means a meaningful fraction of our capacity is being wasted — not because the hardware is inadequate, but because our scheduling is. Jobs are pinned to specific machines by habit. Long-running experiments hog memory they no longer need. Nobody has built a proper queue, so contention is resolved by whoever happens to be loudest in the team channel.

The cheapest capacity we can buy is the capacity we already own. A modest investment in better scheduling — a shared job queue, automatic checkpointing so preemption is safe, memory limits enforced by default — would likely recover twenty to thirty percent of effective throughput at a cost of a few engineer-weeks. Compare that to the alternative: another node costs real capital, ongoing power and cooling, physical space, and, less obviously, more operational surface area. Every machine we add is one more thing that can fail, one more driver version to keep consistent, one more machine whose silent degradation we have to notice. Reliability is not a static property of a fleet; it erodes with size unless we invest in maintaining it, and we have not yet demonstrated that we maintain what we have particularly well.

There's also the question of reversibility, which I think we've underweighted. Buying hardware is a largely one-way door. Resale value on specialised accelerators is poor, the market moves quickly, and a purchase made for today's workload may be poorly matched to whatever we're building in eighteen months. Improving utilisation, by contrast, is almost entirely reversible. If we build a scheduler and it turns out we were wrong about our headroom, we've lost a few weeks and gained a permanent piece of tooling. If we buy a node and we were wrong, we've lost capital and committed ourselves to a physical footprint. When two options have similar expected value, the reversible one should win, because it preserves our ability to learn.

Latency deserves its own word. Some of our pain is not throughput pain at all — it's the interactive experience of a developer waiting for a quick evaluation run. No amount of batch scheduling fixes that, and it's the one argument for dedicated hardware I take seriously. But the right response to interactive latency is probably a small, reserved slice of existing capacity rather than a new node: carve out one GPU for short interactive jobs, protect it fiercely, and let everything else flow through the queue.

So my recommendation is this: spend the next six weeks on utilisation — the queue, checkpointing, the interactive reserve — and set a concrete trigger now. If, after that work, our p95 queue time for batch jobs still exceeds four hours during normal working weeks, we proceed with a hardware purchase, sized to the measured shortfall rather than to the loudest recent frustration. That trigger converts a debate into an experiment, and it means that when we do buy, we'll do it with evidence rather than anecdote.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. Utilisation numbers can mislead; a machine at forty percent average may still be the bottleneck at the moments that matter, and our measurement window may not capture our real demand curve. It's possible we'll do the work and discover we were saturated all along, in which case we'll have spent six weeks learning something we could have bought our way past. I think that risk is acceptable, and cheap relative to the alternative, but I don't think it's zero.

The deeper point is this: a team that can't efficiently use four GPUs will not efficiently use eight. Utilisation work is not a delay to the hardware decision — it's the prerequisite for making that decision well. Let's discuss on Thursday.

— [Name]

**INTERNAL MEMO**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Thursday

---

We've reached the point in our quarterly planning where the hardware question resurfaces, and I want to lay out my thinking before we meet on Tuesday, because the framing we choose matters more than the numbers we'll argue about.

The immediate trigger is familiar: our two A100 nodes are saturated during working hours, inference queues back up in the afternoons, and at least two projects have quietly deprioritised experiments because they couldn't get slots. The instinctive response is to buy a third node. It's the response that makes the pain go away fastest, and I understand the appeal. But I've spent the last week looking at our utilisation telemetry, and I don't think buying is the right first move.

Here's what the data shows. Our aggregate GPU utilisation sits around 38% across a full week. The saturation we all feel is real, but it's concentrated: peak demand runs from roughly 10:00 to 18:00 on weekdays, driven by interactive development and shared inference endpoints, while overnight and weekend capacity sits almost entirely idle. We are, in effect, a company that owns three times the hardware it needs and schedules it as if it owns a third of that. The problem is less about capacity and more about the shape of demand against a fixed supply.

That reframing changes the cost picture considerably. A new A100 node is roughly $180k up front, plus power, cooling, and rack space that our current colocation arrangement prices at a premium. Against that, the utilisation improvements I think are achievable — job scheduling with a proper queue, checkpointing so long training runs can yield to interactive work, batch-size tuning on our inference endpoints, and moving batch analytics to overnight windows — cost mostly engineering time. Two engineers for three to four weeks is a real cost, but it's a fifth of the hardware outlay, and it's work that pays off on whatever hardware we eventually own. If we buy first and optimise later, we will almost certainly never optimise, because the pressure that motivates it will have evaporated.

Latency is the strongest argument for buying, and I want to be honest about it. Interactive work suffers when queues are long, and developer frustration has real, if unmeasured, costs. But most of our latency pain comes from contention, not from absolute throughput limits. A scheduler that guarantees interactive jobs priority, combined with preemption of batch work, addresses the felt problem — waiting — without adding capacity. There will be a transition period of a week or two where the queue is visible and slightly annoying. That's a tolerable price.

Reliability cuts both ways. A third node gives us redundancy we currently lack; if one node fails today, we lose half our capacity and every project stalls. That's a genuine risk, and it's the part of the buy case I take most seriously. But the mitigation is cheaper than a full node: we can negotiate a short-term cloud burst arrangement for failover at a fraction of the capital cost, and revisit it once we see how our demand actually behaves under the new scheduling regime. Paying for reliability as an operating expense, provisionally, is more prudent than buying it as a permanent asset before we understand our true baseline.

The opportunity cost question is the one I keep returning to. $180k spent on a node is $180k not spent on the two product initiatives we've been deferring, and those have clearer paths to revenue than anything the extra hardware would enable. Hardware also depreciates fast in this market; the A100 we'd buy today will be worth markedly less in two years, and the model landscape is shifting quickly enough that our workload mix may look different by then.

Finally, reversibility. Scheduling improvements are reversible in the trivial sense that they're software, but more importantly they're informative: if we optimise and still saturate, we'll have precise data on what to buy and how much. Buying first forecloses that learning. The sequencing matters — optimise, measure for a quarter, then buy with evidence if the need persists.

My recommendation, then: we spend the next month on scheduling and workload shaping, arrange a small cloud burst contract as a reliability backstop, and revisit the purchase decision at the end of the quarter with real numbers in hand. I hold this view with reasonable but not complete confidence — if the scheduling work stalls or our demand grows faster than expected, buying becomes right quickly, and I'd rather we err toward revisiting the decision early than defending it stubbornly.

Please come to Tuesday's meeting with objections, especially from those closest to the daily queue pain. That experience is data too.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Friday

We've reached the point where our inference cluster is saturated during peak hours and idle overnight, and the question on the table is whether we should spend roughly $180K on two additional GPU nodes or invest the next quarter in squeezing more out of the hardware we already own. I want to lay out my thinking on this before we commit, because the two options are not symmetric in cost, risk, or reversibility, and I don't think we've been honest enough about that asymmetry in our discussions so far.

Let's start with the obvious case for buying. Our p99 latency has crept from 400ms to nearly 1.2 seconds over the past two months, and that is no longer an abstract number — the product team has flagged it in two consecutive reviews, and our own internal dashboards show request timeouts climbing in lockstep. Latency degradation of this kind is corrosive in a way that's easy to underestimate: users don't complain loudly, they just quietly use the product less, and by the time the churn shows up in metrics we'll be having a very different and more expensive conversation. Buying capacity is also fast. We can have hardware racked and serving traffic within three weeks, whereas a serious utilisation effort — better batching, dynamic scheduling, quantisation work, model consolidation — is a multi-quarter project with an uncertain payoff. When something is actively hurting, speed of relief has real value.

But the case for buying has a weakness we keep glossing over: our average utilisation sits around 34%. That is not a capacity problem; it is a scheduling problem. We provisioned for peak, which means we paid for the worst hour of the worst day and are now living with the consequences of that decision every other hour. The overnight idle capacity alone, if we shifted batch jobs, fine-tuning runs, and evaluation workloads into it, would effectively give us a second cluster for free. The opportunity cost cuts both ways here. Money spent on new hardware is money not spent on the reliability work we've deferred — better failover, proper capacity monitoring, the redundancy fixes that caused the March incident. And every dollar of hardware we buy that sits at 40% utilisation is a dollar working at less than half its potential, which is the same as paying a full-time engineer to work two hours a day.

There's also the question of what happens if our traffic assumptions are wrong. We're projecting 60% growth based on the sales pipeline, but pipelines slip, and if growth comes in at half that, new hardware becomes a stranded asset depreciating on our books. Conversely, if growth doubles, no amount of clever scheduling saves us and we'll need to buy anyway — but we'll buy then, with better information, having spent a quarter learning exactly where our true bottlenecks are. That's the reversibility argument, and I think it's the strongest one. Scheduling and batching improvements are almost entirely reversible and portable: the work makes our fleet more efficient whether we end up with four nodes or ten, and nothing we learn is wasted. Hardware, once purchased, is largely a sunk commitment — resale value on specialised accelerators is poor, and our procurement cycle means we can't easily unwind a bad purchase.

On reliability, buying more hardware does help in one narrow sense: more nodes means more headroom when one fails. But our actual failure modes in the last two incidents were software — a stuck scheduler and a memory leak — and neither would have been fixed by more iron. Redundancy without operational maturity just means more things that can break.

So here is my recommendation, stated plainly: we do not buy hardware this quarter. Instead, we dedicate two engineers for the next ten weeks to a focused utilisation program — continuous batching, workload shifting into off-peak windows, and quantisation for our two largest models — with a hard checkpoint at the end. If p99 latency is back under 500ms and utilisation is above 55%, we hold. If we've done the work and the numbers say we're still short, we buy, and we'll do it with confidence rather than anxiety.

I want to be clear about the uncertainty in this plan. Utilisation work has a habit of revealing that the last 20% of efficiency is disproportionately hard, and our latency target may prove unreachable on current hardware no matter how well we schedule. There's also execution risk: two engineers on this project are two not doing feature work, and that cost is real even if it doesn't appear on a hardware invoice. If we hit the checkpoint having genuinely tried and fallen short, buying becomes the obvious next step and nobody should feel we wasted a quarter.

The discipline here is to make the cheap, reversible move first, and reserve the expensive, irreversible one for when the evidence demands it. I'd like to align on this in Monday's planning session.

**INTERNAL MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Date:** Thursday

---

We've reached the point in our quarterly planning where the GPU question resurfaces, and I want to lay out my thinking before we meet on Friday. The short version: I think we should spend the next eight weeks seriously improving utilisation of the hardware we already own, and only then decide whether the purchase is genuinely necessary. That's not a hedge — it's a deliberate sequencing decision, and I'll explain why.

First, the case for buying is real, and I don't want to strawman it. Our queue times during the last two model-evaluation sprints were genuinely painful. Researchers waited hours for slots, some experiments were quietly dropped rather than rescheduled, and at least one promising fine-tuning direction was abandoned partly because nobody wanted to fight for compute. If our constraint is peak demand rather than average demand, no amount of scheduling cleverness fixes that. Buying hardware converts a recurring coordination cost into a capital expense, and there's something to be said for removing a whole class of friction from the team's week.

But when I look at our actual telemetry, the picture is less clear-cut than the queue times suggest. Across the fleet, our average utilisation sits somewhere in the low thirties, and even during the crunch weeks we rarely exceeded the mid-fifties. That means the hardware we own is idle more often than it is busy — the pain we feel is a scheduling and allocation problem, not a raw capacity problem. Jobs are pinned to specific machines for historical reasons, long-running inference processes hold memory they no longer need, and nobody owns the job of reclaiming stranded capacity. Buying more hardware in this state would mostly mean buying more idle hardware. It would also mean new failure modes: more machines to patch, more drivers to keep in sync, more physical diversity in a fleet we already struggle to characterise.

Latency cuts both ways here, and it's worth being honest about that. Local hardware gives us predictable, low-latency access, and that predictability has real value for interactive debugging and for the latency-sensitive inference paths serving our internal tools. If improving utilisation means batching more aggressively or time-sharing more aggressively, some interactive workloads will feel it. I think we can protect those paths — they're a small and identifiable fraction of our load — but we should name that risk rather than pretend the change is free.

Cost is where the asymmetry becomes decisive. The purchase we've scoped would consume the better part of two quarters of discretionary budget, plus ongoing power, cooling, and maintenance. Improving utilisation costs mostly engineering time: a proper scheduler, better telemetry, a policy for reclaiming idle allocations, and someone accountable for each of those. That's maybe a fraction of one engineer's quarter. And crucially, the utilisation work is reversible and accumulative. If we invest in scheduling and it turns out we genuinely are capacity-constrained, nothing is wasted — the scheduler makes any future fleet more efficient, and we'll have much better data on what "constrained" actually means. If we buy hardware and it turns out demand was softer than the anecdotes suggested, that capital is sunk. Opportunity cost matters too: the same budget would fund a second engineer for over a year, or a serious investment in our evaluation infrastructure, both of which compound in ways that depreciating silicon does not.

There's also a reliability argument that I think we're underweighting. A larger fleet is not automatically a more reliable one. Right now, a single node failure during a crunch takes out a meaningful fraction of our capacity, and our recovery story is manual. Hardening what we have — better checkpointing, automatic job migration, honest capacity dashboards — improves reliability *and* utilisation simultaneously. Buying more machines before we have those mechanisms just multiplies the surface area of the problem.

So my recommendation is concrete: we commit the next eight weeks to the utilisation track, with a defined target — sustained utilisation above sixty percent and p95 queue times under thirty minutes for batch work — and a hard decision point at the end. If we hit the target and demand still exceeds capacity, I will champion the purchase with real numbers behind it. If we miss the target for reasons that turn out to be structural rather than executional, that itself tells us something important.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. Demand forecasts in this team have a poor track record in both directions, and there's a chance the upcoming evaluation cycle genuinely blows past anything scheduling can absorb. If leadership signals that a major initiative lands next month, we should revisit this immediately rather than dogmatically sticking to the plan. But absent that, the sequencing is clear: understand and use what we own, then buy with confidence rather than anxiety.

Please come to Friday's meeting having read the utilisation dashboard, and push back hard if you think I'm wrong about the peak-versus-average question. That's the crux, and I'd rather settle it with data than with seniority.

**MEMO**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Local AI compute — buy more hardware or use what we have better?
**Date:** Internal circulation only

---

We've reached the point in our capacity planning where the two options on the table — purchasing additional local GPU hardware versus improving utilisation of the machines we already own — need a decision rather than another round of discussion. I've spent the last two weeks looking at our actual usage data, our cost exposure, and the shape of our workload over the next year, and I want to lay out my thinking in full, because this is a decision where the obvious answer and the correct answer are not the same thing.

The case for buying more hardware is easy to make and easy to overstate. Our peak demand periods do saturate the cluster, and when that happens, jobs queue, experiments stall, and people's afternoons disappear into rescheduling. Latency to first token and time-to-result for training runs are both visibly worse during those windows, and there's a real morale cost to a team that spends its day watching a job scheduler. But the peak is the trap. When we look at utilisation across the whole week rather than the worst hours, our fleet sits at roughly 40 percent average utilisation. We are buying, in effect, a car that idles most of the day because a few errands happen at the same time. Adding capacity at the peak would compound that problem, not solve it, and the capital cost is substantial enough that it deserves scrutiny rather than reflexive approval. Hardware also depreciates quickly in this market; a purchase made today to solve a peak problem may be worth a fraction of its cost in eighteen months, and it locks us into a power and cooling footprint we can't easily shed.

The case for improving utilisation is less glamorous but stronger. Most of our gains are available through unglamorous work: better job scheduling, batching inference requests that currently run one at a time, quantising models where quality tolerates it, and moving long-running batch work into overnight and weekend windows that are currently nearly idle. None of this requires new capital. It requires roughly three to four weeks of focused engineering time, which is a real opportunity cost — that's time not spent on product work — but it's a cost we can reverse or abandon if the payoff disappoints, unlike a purchase order. There's also a reliability argument that cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy, and if a node fails today, we feel it. But more machines also means more failure surface, more maintenance, and more of our limited attention spent keeping the lights on. Improving utilisation on a smaller fleet keeps our operational burden where it is while making the fleet we have more dependable in practice, because well-scheduled systems degrade more gracefully than overloaded ones.

That said, I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. Our demand forecast is genuinely fuzzy. If the new product initiative lands the way its advocates hope, inference load could double within two quarters, and no amount of scheduling cleverness will absorb that. If it doesn't, additional hardware would sit mostly idle and we'd have spent money we can't recover. The asymmetry matters: under-utilisation is a waste we can fix later; over-provisioning is a waste we're stuck with. Reversibility should therefore weigh heavily. Scheduling improvements, batching, and quantisation are all reversible decisions. A hardware purchase is largely not — resale value on used accelerators is poor, and the sunk cost follows us.

My recommendation is that we commit to the utilisation track now, with a defined review point. Specifically: we spend the next month on scheduling and batching work, measure the result against our queue-time and latency baselines, and set a concrete trigger — sustained utilisation above roughly 75 percent for four consecutive weeks, or peak queue times exceeding a threshold the team agrees is painful — at which point we revisit the purchase with real data in hand rather than forecasts. This isn't a refusal to buy hardware; it's sequencing. If growth arrives, we'll buy, and we'll buy knowing exactly what we need. If it doesn't, we'll have saved a significant sum and learned something about our own workload in the process.

I'd like to discuss this at Thursday's sync. If anyone has data that contradicts the utilisation figures, now is the time to surface it — the whole argument rests on them.
